newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hong Kong lures Japan's working women.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong lures Japan's working women.

text.p: While dim sum feasts and designer fashions draw most of the millions of Japanese who visit Hong Kong each year, a growing number of women are following job offers -- not tour guides -- to the city.

Thousands of women have moved from Japan to Hong Kong since the early 1990s, and they stand apart both from expatriates sent by Japanese firms operating there and from the thousands of Southeast Asian women who work as housekeepers in the colony.
The expatriates -- blue-suited businessmen from blue chip firms -- command high pay and perks like housing and home trips. The maids also earn much more than they could at home.
In contrast, many of the Japanese women who move to Hong Kong are seeking not money but an escape from the so-called glass ceiling at home as well as a new lifestyle.
"More than salary, it's the opportunity to build oversees career experiences these Japanese women seek," said Yuko Nakase, a spokeswoman for Pasona Inc, a major recruiting firm in Tokyo.
"Others simply love Hong Kong and everything about it."

The Tokyo-based job-placement firm has operated in Hong Kong since 1983, catering mainly to Japanese firms that set up shop in the colony in growing numbers as Japan's yen appreciated and the China market grew more attractive.

Japanese women's desire to work in Hong Kong picked up in the early 1990s, when Japan's economic slowdown began to pinch demand for clerical and temporary staff, mostly female positions that were the first targets of cost-cutting measures.

Sensing a market match, Pasona in 1993 began holding a series of Hong Kong job fairs in Japan, drawing over a thousand potential applicants, many of them women. Of 802 who formally sought work in Hong Kong through Pasona in 1996, 75 percent were female, the company said.
Working in Hong Kong is also a way out for women frustrated by Japan's notorious male-dominated corporate culture.

"Japanese women who have studied abroad and achieved a command of English hope to use it in their careers, but they find that overwhelmingly Japanese companies only give foreign postings to male employees," Nakase said.

Japanese jobseekers with work experience and basic clerical skills find strong demand from Japan firms which seek to save money by hiring locally and which find Japanese workers easier to communicate with than local Hong Kong staff.
Jobs on offer are typically clerical, with more challenging opportunities -- and better pay -- offered to those with good computer skills or command of English or Chinese.
"The ideal recruit would have good English, business experience including a command of Japanese business etiquette, and increasingly, Mandarin Chinese," Pasona's spokeswoman said.
With China set to take over the British colony on July 1, demand has grown sharply for Japanese applicants with Mandarin Chinese, the official dialect of China.
With Sino-Japanese economic ties growing, Chinese language studies have boomed among Japanese, even replacing English in popularity according to some recent surveys.

Japanese have few problems with written Chinese because it shares most characters and a considerable vocabulary with the Japanese language, but struggle mightily to pronounce Chinese well enough to be understood.
